Title: Cancer Overview
Source:

Last Updated: 2024–2026

---

Overview
- Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably. - These cells can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymph system. - The spread of cancer to distant organs is called metastasis, and it is a major cause of cancer-related death. How cancer develops
- Cancer often starts with changes in a cell's DNA. - DNA changes can happen because of errors during cell division, harmful exposures such as tobacco smoke or radiation, inherited mutations, infections, and environmental or lifestyle factors. - As abnormal cells continue to divide, they may form tumors and spread through the bloodstream or lymphatic system. Common types
- There are more than 100 types of cancer. - Carcinoma begins in epithelial cells and includes lung, breast, and colorectal cancer. - Sarcoma develops in bones, muscles, fat, or connective tissues. - Leukemia affects blood-forming tissues such as the bone marrow and blood cells. - Lymphoma affects the lymphatic system and immune cells. - Melanoma develops in pigment-producing cells called melanocytes. Cancer statistics
- In 2022, there were about 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide. - Lung cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 2022 and the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. - Other common cancers include breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach cancer. - Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. - About 400,000 children develop cancer each year worldwide. Main risk factors
- Cancer risk factors increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not guarantee that a person will get cancer.

breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach cancer. - Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. - About 400,000 children develop cancer each year worldwide. Main risk factors - Cancer risk factors increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not guarantee that a person will get cancer. - Risk rises with age. - Tobacco use strongly increases cancer risk. - Heavy alcohol use raises the risk of several cancers. - Family history and inherited gene changes can increase risk. - Excess body weight and low physical activity increase the risk of several cancers. - UV exposure from sunlight or tanning beds increases skin cancer risk. - Infections such as HPV can increase cancer risk. - Environmental exposures such as radon, asbestos, secondhand smoke, and certain chemicals can raise risk. Prevention strategies
- Avoid tobacco and secondhand smoke. - Maintain a healthy weight. - Be physically active. - Eat a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and beans. - Limit alcohol. - Protect yourself from the sun. - Get vaccinated against HPV and hepatitis B when appropriate. - Use screening tests such as mammograms, Pap tests, colonoscopy, and low-dose CT when recommended.

Last Updated:  January 1, 2026

---

TNM staging system
- TNM is a standard system for describing how far a cancer has spread. - T means the size and extent of the primary tumor. - N means whether nearby lymph nodes contain cancer. - M means whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. - TX means the primary tumor cannot be assessed. - T0 means there is no evidence of a primary tumor. - Tis means carcinoma in situ, which is early cancer limited to the original cell layer. - T1 through T4 mean increasing size or local spread of the tumor. - NX means nearby lymph nodes cannot be assessed. - N0 means no cancer is found in nearby lymph nodes. - N1 through N3 mean increasing spread to nearby lymph nodes. - M0 means no distant metastasis is detected. - M1 means the cancer has spread to distant organs or tissues. - TNM is often written as a combination such as T2N1M0. - In that example, the tumor is moderately sized, there is lymph node involvement, and there is no distant metastasis. - TNM is especially used for solid tumors. Stage 0 to stage 4
- Stage 0 is also called carcinoma in situ. - Stage 0 means abnormal cells are present but have not spread into nearby tissue. - Stage 1 means the cancer is small and confined to the original site. - Stage 1 usually means there is little or no spread to nearby lymph nodes.

is also called carcinoma in situ. - Stage 0 means abnormal cells are present but have not spread into nearby tissue. - Stage 1 means the cancer is small and confined to the original site. - Stage 1 usually means there is little or no spread to nearby lymph nodes. - Stage 2 means the tumor is larger than stage 1 or has started to spread into nearby tissue or a small number of nearby lymph nodes. - Stage 3 means the cancer has grown deeper into nearby tissues and may involve more nearby lymph nodes, but it has not spread to distant organs. - Stage 4 means the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. - Stage 4 is also called metastatic cancer. - Stage 4 cancer can spread to organs such as the lungs, liver, bones, or brain. How staging affects treatment
- Stage 0 and stage 1 cancers are often treated with local treatments such as surgery, radiation, or both. - Stage 2 and stage 3 cancers often need a combination of treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. - Stage 4 cancers usually need systemic therapy such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy. - Staging also helps doctors estimate prognosis, plan follow-up, and decide whether the goal is cure, long-term control, or symptom relief. Grading vs staging
- Staging describes how much cancer is in the body and where it has spread. - Grading describes how abnormal the cancer cells look under the microscope. - Lower-grade cancers look more like normal cells. - Higher-grade cancers look more abnormal and are often more aggressive. Why accurate staging matters
- Accurate staging helps doctors choose the right treatment. - Under-staging can lead to treatment that is too weak.

Title: Cancer Symptoms
Source:
- https://www.cancer.org/cancer/diagnosis-staging/signs-and-symptoms-of-cancer.html
- https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/early-cancer-warning-signs-5-symptoms-you-shouldnt-ignore

- https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/spot-cancer-early/why-is-early-diagnosis-important

Last Updated: 2026

---

General warning signs
- Unexplained weight loss or weight change can be a warning sign. - Fatigue that does not improve with rest can be concerning. - A new lump or swelling should be checked. - Unusual bleeding or discharge can be a warning sign. - A sore that does not heal needs evaluation. - Changes in bowel or bladder habits can matter. - Persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing should not be ignored. - Skin changes, including a changing mole or new skin lesion, can be important. - These symptoms do not always mean cancer. - The key concern is whether the symptom is new, persistent, or getting worse. Common symptoms by cancer type
- Lung cancer may cause persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, frequent lung infections, or hoarseness. - Breast cancer may cause a lump in the breast or underarm, changes in breast shape or size, nipple discharge, or skin dimpling and redness. - Colorectal cancer may cause blood in stool, persistent diarrhea or constipation, abdominal pain or bloating, unexplained weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. - Prostate cancer may cause difficulty urinating, frequent urination, blood in urine or semen, pelvic discomfort, a weak urine stream, trouble starting urination, or pain when urinating. - Skin cancer may cause new or changing moles, irregular borders, uneven color, sores that do not heal, or unusual skin color changes. - Cervical or endometrial cancer may cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, pain during intercourse, unusual vaginal discharge, or bleeding after menopause. - Ovarian cancer may cause bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly, appetite changes, or urinary changes.

sores that do not heal, or unusual skin color changes. - Cervical or endometrial cancer may cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, pain during intercourse, unusual vaginal discharge, or bleeding after menopause. - Ovarian cancer may cause bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly, appetite changes, or urinary changes. - Pancreatic cancer may cause upper abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, poor appetite, new diabetes, or jaundice. - Liver cancer may cause jaundice, abdominal swelling or pain, loss of appetite, fatigue, or weakness. - Stomach cancer may cause persistent indigestion, loss of appetite, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, or feeling full quickly after eating. - Lymphoma or leukemia may cause swollen lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, fatigue, frequent infections, easy bruising, or unexplained weight loss. Early detection importance
- Early detection matters because cancer found sooner is usually smaller and easier to treat. - Treatment is often more effective when cancer is still at an early stage. - Early treatment can offer more options, including local treatment such as surgery. - Early detection can reduce treatment intensity, side effects, and long-term complications. - Early detection can improve survival and quality of life. - Screening can find some cancers before symptoms appear. - New symptoms should also be checked early because some cancers do not cause obvious symptoms until they are advanced. When to seek medical attention
- Seek medical attention for a new lump or swelling. - Seek medical attention for unexplained weight loss. - Seek medical attention for persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing. - Seek medical attention for unusual bleeding or discharge. - Seek medical attention for a sore that does not heal. - Seek medical attention for changes in bowel or bladder habits. - Seek medical attention for ongoing pain without a clear cause.

Symptom variations by stage
- Early stage cancers may cause no symptoms or only subtle local signs. - Middle stage cancers are more likely to cause pain, swelling, cough, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or enlarged lymph nodes. - Advanced stage cancers are more likely to cause fatigue, weight loss, poor appetite, persistent pain, and symptoms from distant spread such as shortness of breath, jaundice, bone pain, headaches, or seizures.

Last Updated: 2026

---

Surgery
- Surgery can remove the whole tumor, remove part of a tumor to reduce symptoms, or take tissue for diagnosis and staging. - Surgery is a local treatment and works best for solid tumors in one area. - Curative surgery aims to remove all visible cancer. - Debulking surgery removes as much cancer as possible when full removal is not possible. - Palliative surgery helps relieve pain, pressure, bleeding, or blockage. - Diagnostic or staging surgery helps confirm cancer and see how far it has spread. - Surgery is often combined with chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy. - Surgery is usually not enough by itself for cancers that have spread widely. Chemotherapy
- Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing and dividing. - It targets rapidly dividing cells and can shrink tumors or slow cancer spread. - Chemotherapy may be given before surgery, after surgery, together with radiation, or to control cancer that has spread. - Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, mouth sores, hair loss, low blood counts, infection risk, constipation or diarrhea, and nerve tingling. - If a tumor is too large for surgery at first, chemotherapy may be used first to make it smaller. Radiation therapy
- Radiation therapy uses high-energy radiation, usually X-rays, to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. - It damages the DNA of cancer cells so they can no longer divide normally. - Radiation may be the main treatment, or it may be used before surgery, after surgery, together with chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms.

9.content:
radiation, usually X-rays, to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. - It damages the DNA of cancer cells so they can no longer divide normally. - Radiation may be the main treatment, or it may be used before surgery, after surgery, together with chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms. - External beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body. - Internal radiation therapy, also called brachytherapy, places radioactive material inside or near the tumor. - Common side effects depend on the treatment area and may include skin irritation, tiredness, appetite loss, nausea, and local tissue inflammation. Immunotherapy
- Immunotherapy helps the body’s immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. - It can boost immune activity, remove the brakes on immune cells, or give the immune system agents that help it attack cancer more effectively. - Main types include checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T or T-cell therapy, monoclonal antibodies, and cancer vaccines. - Immunotherapy is often used for cancers that have spread, come back, or do not respond well to other treatments. - Side effects can include fatigue, skin changes, flu-like symptoms, and inflammation in organs such as the lungs, liver, intestines, or thyroid. Targeted therapy
- Targeted therapy uses drugs to attack specific molecules, genes, or proteins that help cancer cells grow and spread. - It is designed to hit a more specific cancer feature than standard chemotherapy. - Targeted therapy may block growth signals, stop tumor cells from dividing, or cut off blood vessel growth. - It is often used when the cancer has a known biomarker or mutation. - Main types include monoclonal antibodies and small-molecule drugs. - Common side effects include skin problems, diarrhea, and high blood pressure. - Not every cancer has a targetable mutation, and some cancers can develop resistance over time.

Combination treatments
- Combination treatments use two or more cancer therapies together. - Combining treatments can improve effectiveness, reduce resistance, and treat both local and spread disease. - Neoadjuvant therapy is given before surgery to shrink a tumor. - Adjuvant therapy is given after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells. - Concurrent therapy gives treatments at the same time, such as chemotherapy with radiation. - Combination treatment can be more effective, but it may also cause more side effects. Clinical trials
- Clinical trials are research studies in people that test new ways to prevent, detect, diagnose, or treat cancer. - They help determine whether a new treatment is safe and effective. - Main types include treatment trials, prevention trials, screening or diagnostic trials, and supportive care trials. - Trial phases usually move from safety and dose testing to efficacy testing and then comparison with standard care. - Clinical trials are not only for people with no other options.
